p: Yeah, so as you know, so many of the uhm, so many of these conversations are ongoing with OMB. These things have come up and we have constant conversations around them.

I’m glad the conversations are happening. No, for a program, you know the Council often uhm initiates these important programs and show how important they are and that they work. Uhm, and it should be picked up by the Administration from this point going forward, especially since it’s being implemented and expanded widely.
Appreciate that, yup.
Thank you. I’ll turn it over to Council Member Joseph.

Thank you Chair. Uhm, my next topic is something that we haven’t touched on and need to really look at it and see how we could come up with a comprehensive plan, right? Chronic absenteeism, we have not addressed that. I’d like to know what is your plan. For example, students in temporary housing, they are 56 percent of chronic

absenteeism. What is the plan? I know we have shelter based coordinators. That’s something the Council worked with the Administration. We must get our students back into school. Are we using every tool in our toolbox? Are we partnering with social workers, parent coordinators, to make sure that the students are in school and what- whatever the barrier is, are we working to remove those barriers?

Yeah, look chronic absenteeism is a huge one. It’s a huge issue for us and you’ve gone directly to our most vulnerable young people but I’ll tell you across every single demographic in our city, one thing that is clear about our young people and families right now is that our students are attending school for fewer days than they did prior to the pandemic. We’ve seen an increase in attendance and a decrease in chronic absenteeism over the last number of years but this is a citywide issue, a statewide issue and a national issue. And so, we have to make sure that we are very clear around how we’re getting to our most vulnerable young people. What we’ve done uh, is one of the things that we’ve done is to shift our attendance teachers to superintendent to be supervised by superintendents as

opposed to like more essential supervision and I think that’s yielded some really good results because then you’re closer to the community of schools that you have to visit and that you - and that supervision has been strong. But I want to turn it over-

What’s the current caseload for a shelter based coordinator? What’s the current caseload? Because that also will help determine if you don’t have enough, then you’re not reaching everyone that you should be reaching and students in temporary housing, we should not only be buying stuff for them. What are we doing to support them academically?
Yeah and when you talk about every child and families that we’re thinking, we’re continuing. I think that’s important there but Flavia can address it.

Absolutely. Thank you Council Member Joseph for the question. Uh, so let me start by addressing the question about the ratio. So, we have 180 community coordinators supporting our shelters and this is nearly 300 shelters. So, even though some of the shelters, the hotels, have moved

now and they’re taking over uhm, managed by the Department of Homeless Services, still a ratio could improve but I think it’s really looking at like all the ecosystem of support, where I do want to begin by addressing is that while there is significant work to do in this area, uhm, we went from having nearly 41 percent of the students in the whole system being chronically absent to 33.3 percent. So, 7.4 percent reduction.
Well, your students in temporary housing are still at 56 percent.

Students in temporary housing - absolutely, it went, it went - you are correct. When you look at all STH, we started with 54.2 percent of them being chronically absent and now we are 48 percent. So, 5.5 percent reduction and the only subgroup in our system where we actually have lower chronic absenteeism than what we had prepandemic, it’s students in foster care, which is a direct correlation of the investment that was done with your partnership of creating an office of foster care, which is one of probably the only two offices across the nation, small but mighty dedicating to these supports.

So, I think what we see here is when we invest, we see a return for our investment. I also don’t want to miss this opportunity to highlight the critical work that community schools and looking at wraparound supports provide to mitigating challenges of chronic absenteeism. When we look at our data and we look at the recent calls, we look at national research. Why are students out? There’s three factors that come up often. One of them is when students are chronically ill and have other circumstances that keep them from coming. Another one is uhm, aversion, which includes mental health challenges. Students who just like feel like they don’t belong. That they - you know they’d rather stay home and not be in school. Then the third one is disengagement and disengagement ranges from not having that adult connection to also not being challenged or being supported by the content. So, when we talk about combating chronic absenteeism in addition to increasing the support, the magic is, our school communities need to know every child well.

Are we - are we doing that training? It can’t happen by a wand. Is that conversation happening? Are we engaging families and parents and school based- are agencies talking to each other? Is DHS talking to you? Is ACS talking to you? So, these things need to happen.

Absolutely, 100 percent and I just uhm, had a meeting with leadership but DH- uh last week. We continue to meet with them. We are also discussing when we - which was a good thing, close in the hotels to move students to more stable homes but that also created challenges in terms of now we have children in the middle of the school and at different times, that are having to move from where they were and while they continue to be allowed to remain in the school that they were currently enrolled, that also creates another set of challenges. So, I agree with you 100 percent and I’m committed that this is work that needs to be done in an interagency support, but also, we need to be really pointed about what are the root causes why children are out.
Thank you. Thank you Council Member Joseph.
Thank you.
Council Member Wong.

Thank you Chair. Uhm, I want to, uh, start with uh, the Summer Rising Program because uh, I again, as a member of the CEC, I was visiting schools and I hear a lot of feedback from parents. Uhm, what happens is the attendance of the Summer Rising program drops significantly after the first week and I - it’s always my belief that either DOE or somebody from the school would reach out to the students. Hey, you know, you should come to school. And if you’re not, reach down the others on the waiting list that want to come to school. But I just don’t - I didn’t see that. I didn’t see that for several summers, so can you talk about your remedies because it’s just, just really it stresses me to see a school open but so few kids attending Summer Rising. Can you- can you address that?

Yeah, so first of all, Summer Rising is a wonderful program that we are happy to make available for parents-parents. It's universally

a very popular program for families but you do raise a significant concern. The attendance in Summer Rising is not based on a mandated, a mandatory program for families, so it ranges in the mid-60 percent in terms of attendance overall and I do believe that’s a constant concern for us, partly because you know many of our families sign up and they - they know that they have gaps in the summer. They might be going place- they might be doing other things and so, it’s very difficult then to give a new spot to families but we are constantly working with our schools. Our schools are really thinking about ways to make sure we’re serving as many families as possible. And so, I want to turn it over to Kevin to add anything else there.

Yes and Council Member Wong, as mentioned earlier as a follow up to your question, it was a relocation within the building at 96. One of our rooftop units had a fan issue. The CO2 readers were detected in the classroom, so we relocated out. FDNY cleared it and we went back in.

That was fixed, yes absolutely. As it relates to Summer Rising, by the way for all here and watching at home, the deadline for applications is March 27th. So, encourage friends, families and others to apply. Uhm, we’re very excited about the program. We, at the end of every year, work with our research and policy group to survey families, to talk a little bit about what’s it - you know what do you like in the program? Where should we improve and I do note like the Chancellor, parents do have commitments through the summer season that sometimes draw them away from the program. With that being said, we’ll continue to work with our CBO partners and DYCD to increase outreach to families to make sure we’re filling the seats, the 110,000 seats we’re offering. And across our sites, we’re increasing our sites from 360 to 379, so hopefully we’ll reach families where they are to lead any transportation issues traveling to and from.

Thank you and onto topics, difficult topics, hold harmless policy. Uhm, DOE has continued a hold harmless funding model where schools were declining enrollment maintain their budgets.

Uh, at point do we acknowledge that we’re funding empty seats and is there a long term plan to phase this out or this is now a permanent policy? Can anybody answer that?

I will attempt to but uhm, but you’re raising like Council Member Restler did uh, earlier, the- the difficulty of this time and this - and that proposal or that policy and so, we’re continuing to have those difficult conversations within uh DOE and no decision has been made on hold harmless and we’ll continue to work with our City Hall partners as well as uhm OMB to think it through.
So, is there a plan to phase this out or this is now permanent?

No decisions have been made. We’re going to continue to have conversations as you know, the projections that’s used to calculate hold harmless we’ll figure out down the line. And so, uhm, this is the time to have the conversation uhm and we’re continuing to think about that.

Okay, yeah moving on. Uhm, it is difficult to talk about this but is - it’s a fact that we have schools that are underenrolled and I’ve been keeping track of them. There are schools

that enroll fewer than 150 kids compared to four or five years ago where there’s several hundred kids. Uh, uh, is consolidation being actively considered where there are multiple underenrolled schools in close proximities?

Yeah, so first of all Council Member Wong, thank you for the question. It is a tough question but I don’t think it’s uh it’s a secret to anyone. We’ve lost over 200,000 kids and so, if we’re going to lose a high number of students, it’s going to impact many of our schools and it’s going to impact uhm, our schools that serve demographically families who are leaving the city. Uh, more - it’s going to impact them uhm disproportionately right and so, we have seen significant numbers of schools declining enrollment. When I look at uhm, across our city, I do think we’re going to be discussing having serious conversations about areas that we can see opportunities for like you said, consolidations and so on. And that’s also a part and part and parcel of thinking about the noncapital strategies as it pertains for our plan for class size.
Thank you Council Member.
Thank you Chair. Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Restler.
Terrific. Uhm, thank you Chair. I really appreciate it and uh I tried to go to Parks but there were too many people, so I came back to have fun with you guys.
More people at Parks than here? No, I’m kidding.

You know, well you got started early. Uhm, so I wanted to ask about a few things. Firstly, I just you know it feels like things are really moving in the right direction on early childhood, which is great on a number of different fronts and I’m so thankful that we have more seats coming in. Greenpoint in 11222 in Brooklyn Heights and the surrounding neighborhoods in 11201, in 11217, a lot of District 33 is covered. We did send a request for data. Perhaps we were not clear. We didn’t get all of the data we requested so I’m just going to follow up. I don’t think it was intentional but DC Hawkins, I will bug you about that later today. Thank you in advance.

Uhm but thank you for all the progress in early childhood. This is the first time where I didn’t just spend almost all my time complaining about it in the last - in four years.
How can - now you can pay attention to your own early childhood.

There we go. That’s it, you know. I want to shift to class size which I’m very anxious about and just there are a number of schools in my district that are struggling on compliance. There was including some of the District 13 schools that you know well Chancellor. Uhm, so last year schools were able to apply for and a number received additional funds to facilitate class size compliance. Are those commitments, multiyear commitments or school- I know schools are applying again for new ways to - for resources to help with compliance with the law. But will they ha- are the- are the funds that they received last year in place for next year as well?
Yeah, because they hired a teacher right, so you can’t hire a teacher for one year.
Right.
Yeah.

I imagine you’re tracking like I’m tracking, losses of art, music, libraries and other you know really, you know essential enrichment programs that are no longer able to be accommodate by some schools to comply with the class size law. Are - how is that - well, let me actually ask the question. How is that being tracked across the system and how concerned are you about this?
Yeah, so when it comes to uh, uhm, you know what you’re talking about arts and uhm you know - those, those programmings that in many of our schools is a huge part of the identity of the school.
100 percent.

Uhm, we do have to uhm manage a local conversation with superintendents, so I’ll give you an example, when I was a superintendent thinking about uhm a particular school. Uhm, we decided that we were going to go in the way of truncating the middle school of that school because it was honor enrolled and we wanted- because, partly because we wanted to protect their OPT room. We wanted to

protect their theater room and their arts programming. And similarly, uhm when we look at uh, another program in my district, in order to instead of doing that, we decided we’re going in my old district side, we’re going to do a proposal to recite a, a, middle school so that the elementary school there could keep those pieces of programming. I really do think it’s very critical that we are having that conversation locally because SOTs and schools and superintendents and principals can often make the best decision based on what they see in front of them. And I'll turn it over to Erin to add anything around specialty rooms as well.
Just briefly if you can because I got a minute and 30 and -

I’ll be quick. Uhm, hi, uh Erin Jahant. Thank you for the question. Uhm, FY27 the way we design the survey, we ask the principals uhm ask for resources that would result in no program reduction. So, they were intentional on how they asked. Additionally, where there were requests for room conversions, we were clear. No reduction in programming in that and then we’re doing secondary uh secondary looks at that with the - we’re not reducing

- uh, we’re not converting classrooms that would otherwise be art rooms or specialty programs.

I mean, I can tell you I’ve got schools that are losing our rooms, losing technology rooms. That has already happened and there’s more that are going to happen to comply. I want us to reduce class sizes but I want to also protect these programs. So, I just, I appreciate the approach that this previous and the current administration are taking of asking principals and school leadership teams, what can - what do you want to do? How can you comply? What recommendations you have, they know best about their schools but there’s a tension here that I’m very concerned about and I’m not really hearing how we’re solving for it. Just a little bit more broadly, I really struggled with the previous Administration on citing new schools, on class size compliance challenges, where SCA was involved. And I think part of the challenge was that SCA had a direct reporting line into City Hall and wasn’t reporting into the DOE or didn’t have a dotted line to the Chancellor and it was immensely frustrating. We had school options for

new schools in Williamsburg that are desperately needed that were just reject- that were in new developments that were rejected without ever talking to me or anyone in my community that were agreed to in rezonings. So, I’m just trying to understand as I look ahead, I’ve got high schools that are bursting at the seams where we need new space. Where they need to grow at the Harry Van Arsdale Campus. I’ve got needs for new elementary school capacity in District 14 in Northern Greenpoint and in the north side of Williamsburg. I’ve got a meeting set up on Wednesday with the folks from district planning but who should I be really coordinating with at the most senior level in the Chancellor’s office on these issues if we’re not getting cooperation from SCA, which hopefully that will change. It’s a new Administration but who should we be coordinating with on these issues?
That would be Deputy Chancellor uhm, Kevin Moran.
Okay. Kevin, we will be in touch. Always good to see you all. Thank you very much.
Thank you Council Member. Council Member Won.

Thank you so much Chair Dinowitz. I want to go back to talking about equity in due process cases. So, formerly known as Carter cases. I’ve been having a lot of conversations with our parents who have special needs, so especially children who are twice exceptional, who just have not been able to find a school that is adequate for their needs. What is the long term plan here because it takes a lot - it costs a lot of money for these parents to have the lawyer to sue and it just is not sustainable long term. What is the Department of Education or New York City Public Schools long term strategy to meet the needs of twice exceptional kids and not just punting them to private schools to meet their needs?

Yes, it’s a great question and we’ve had uhm, and certainly as a superintendent had several conversations with uh - with families who were in that position and really, it boiled down to a really thoughtful approach from each school to meet individual needs but uhm, I’m sure there are more - there’s more of this happening across city and I just

want to turn it over to Christina Foti to address that.

You know Council Member Won, we’ve done so much work on the autism front given the explosion in autism numbers we’re seeing nationally and locally uhm and the next layer of our work really has to focus on neurodiversity and which is often what we’re seeing with our choice exceptional students. Uhm, what we’ve been doing is taking components of what we see kids struggle with, sensory issues and executive function and doing widescale training on both of those things. So, for example, this year, we did 2,127 attendees for executive function training. The reason why this is important is that we’ve never did - done a citywide effort to help educators know how to develop skills that twice exceptional students often struggle with. The same with our sensory spaces and you mentioned those before. I was delighted to hear. Uhm, it’s another area that our twice exceptional students often struggle with. And as you know, the priority is making sure that kids have both the social, emotional, the academic, and uhm the special

education expertise all in one building. As the Chancellor said, this is often done locally. I just wanted to share some of the things that we’re doing systemically.
So, you want to bring the students back to public schools and you’re preparing for it?
Absolutely.
Because I know the governor has asked for due process cases for the cost of it to be brought down. So, what is the plan here during a budget crisis to bring that price down?

Yeah, it’s exactly what we talked about earlier is opening up more of the programs that parents are asking for. And as we spoke about earlier, investments in those programming allows us to expand and those are the most competitive options to allow for families to seek - who want to seek a public school placement.
So, for School District 30 and you- and District 24, you have plans in place to expand those programs for the children?

Yeah, you probably know how much expansion we’ve done in both of those districts.

It’s pretty phenomenal work that most of them have been doing and again, with additional uhm, additional funding for specialized programs, we’re able to do that expansion.
Okay. Can you give me a dollar amount of how much more we can expect this fiscal year coming up?
Uhm, I certainly in terms of what we’re going to be doing this year to expand specialized programs, a dollar amount?
Within the school district, more District 30 and District 24.
Either uhm, our CFO can do that or we can get back to you.

So, we continue to have ongoing conversations around specialized programming with City Hall and OMB and so I don’t have a particular dollar amount for you especially specific to the district. We can uh get back to you but again, these are ongoing conversations that we are having about these important investments.

Okay, I just want to make sure that’s it’s on your radar that District 30 and District 24 has seen a tripling of the number of

students who need these programs, so we want to see at least double of what the funding has been in the upcoming fiscal year.
I’ll be sure to let OMB know that.

And can you help me understand, I know Deputy Chancellor Hawkins is here and we’re so grateful for your partnership for having increased our school seats for 3K and PreK by over 175 in District 30 and District 24 but we want to understand, right now I’m getting a lot of emails and phone calls from early childhood providers who are elated with the news from the Mayor and the Governor saying that we’re going to have full funding for 3K and PreK across the whole entire city. So, right now, from my conversations with the early childhood education providers is that they have submitted an RFI but they have not been given an RFP but it seems that parents and providers are under the impression that we’re going to be opening these 3K and Pre K seats by the fall. So, can you help me understand because you and I have been on the phone multiple times where we know how long the RFP process takes from an RFI to an RFP to all of the approvals

and permits from Department of Education, Department of Health and Mental Hygiene and FDNY, DOB. So, how are we going to do this by fall and what is the plan here and strategy for how we’re going to have children enroll into those schools by the fall because it’s not on My Schools NYC for them to have applied to it. So, just trying to understand your process here.

No, I appreciate those questions. And so, the RFP process to your point, is very involved and that is something we are planning for the future. That would be a larger procurement effort that is not available right now to your point. What we did release to leverage this opportunity to launch 2K and expand 3K in places where we don’t currently have a contract or don’t currently have care in a district school setting was release a request for interest. And so, we are - that RFI you mentioned. In addition to that, we did send surveys to family childcare networks and contracted CBOs to determine if they would like to also participate in the 2K and 3K effort and or right?

And so, what we are doing is two things, leveraging existing contracts, where we can convert underutilized seats to support either and, 2K and 3K where appropriate looking at for 3K specifically, application data where there’s been a history of unmet demand where we can place seats. We also believe in continuity of care. So, where we may launch 2K in the fall, we are looking at providers and locations that already have a permit. To your point, it is a big lift to get permitted by our lovely health department partners, not to their fault and so, we are planning forward for that for year 2 of 2K and in supporting 3K along the way. So, right now, we’re leveraging existing contracts, existing spaces with 3K and also school setting, so District Schools and PreK centers.
So, am I understanding correctly that by fall, these 3K seats will be open?

That’s, that’s our commitment and so and like years prior, if there are new sites that come online, sorry Chair. Sites that come online after the 3K and PreK application process, we notify families through an alert system through My

Schools and then families can always add themselves to the waitlist but it is a rolling process.

Okay because I just want to put on record, Bean Sprout and Woodside is waiting for the 3K seat, especially because we’re getting rid of the Mosaic 3K seat and PreK seat to be out of the district, as we’ve talked about before. So, Bean Sprout has to be that replacement if you close Mosaic and Bunny Hill, that is open in Long Island City that we were able to get open for 3K and PreK. They have a site in Greenpoint and currently Greenpoint only has only one 3K and One PreK. So, they have responded to the RFI and are waiting for it and also, Kuei Luck that is operational in Long Island City, is also in Greenpoint looking to open up a 3K and PreK seat as well. So, I really hope we can get that done. Thank you so much.
Thank you Council Member.
Thank you. Thank you Council Member. Council Member Felder.

Yeah, I apologize. We have you know other votes uh, uh, so I’m sorry I left in the middle.

So, first of all, congratulations and good luck to the whole team because you know that you’re going to get the complaints. You’re not going to get any complements or anything like that and that’s the way it works.
Yeah.

So, I am sorry. That shouldn’t count towards the time. Yeah, but you know my mother, may she rest in peace, till the day she passed away said that the best time of her life was the time she spent in the public school in the Bronx. That’s where she went. That was the - and uh, I always thought that I was the baby and that she would say something else but that’s what it was. So, I’m going to mention three items, not to debate. I’m just asking you to look into them and then one, which I think and I’m going to try to talk as quickly as my colleague did. So, number one, is that the issue of the school yards. I'm not sure you’re aware of it but there used to be a policy where the school yards were entirely dedicated for play for the children. Somehow after the Bloomberg Administration, the - the parts of the school yards have been set aside for parking. I know

that it’s difficult for staff and whatever else to find parking but at the same time, I know that it’s impossible for children to find any place to play. So, I would just ask you to look back to that policy and there is no perfect solution but I would just say is that if you had to take you know - make a choice, I think the school yard should be dedicated entirely, entirely for children to be able to play, one. Two, safety, as it stands now, I- I’ve tried by the way. I can walk into almost any public school that I did and uh, let me tell ya, I’m a scary guy. You know, God forbid the resource officers are not armed. I know it’s a complicated issue but they’re not armed. Anybody God forbid could walk into a public school and we don’t want to wait. I’m just saying my own opinion. You don’t want to wait till something terrible happens. I know it’s - again, I know it’s a complicated issue but right now, anybody could get into the door and they’re not armed. There’s really nothing much they can do. That’s number two. Number three, the public school system used to have many more, a much more I should say - many more options of vocational programs. Now there’s a guy

named Simcha Felder who was always in the principal's office, always. School and I did not get along. It wasn’t my fault, it was their fault. If I had had a vocational program, I would have done very well. And I think that there are many students no matter how many times they give them the tests, it’s just never - it’s not going to work. They’re not made for it so I would just ask that you look into that you know about increasing it. I still haven't graduated, so I’m interested in the program. And finally, the question I really have is the following. Is that this is not something obviously that happened just now but it’s a problem that’s been going on for many years. The issue of the overwhelming need to address the payments and the whole system for special education children in public schools and in non public schools. Time and time again, I’ve heard from parents and providers in schools you know less so, that - denied services. They go through the whole system. There’s something wrong with you know, there really is. It’s broken. Uh, and I can’t blame, I can’t even complain or blame anyone at the Department of Education because it’s an overwhelming problem that never ever, it just

keeps on building you know. It’s never been addressed. So, I have to ask you know, I’m just asking like one provider as an example, it encores one provider, a private - they’re owed an excess of $5 million you know. And I’m just saying to you, maybe it’s not an answer, a question you know that you can answer. I’m just saying that there - I - among the many other things that you have to fix, you know maybe, maybe you can please dedicate - I have some ideas for you by the way that I’m willing to volunteer.
Good, there’s a lot of issues there. Do you want to respond or answer to -
Yeah, yeah, yeah, no, I told him he doesn’t have to respond to the first four.
Okay.
And even the fifth, he doesn’t have to respond. You know what I mean.

I think you know we talked a little bit earlier about due process and reimbursements and there are significant, uhm, issues there. We’re making significant headway on those though and I think the more we can, we can really

attack some of the core issues, the better it will be for efficiency long term.

I’m not allowed to say anything but if the Chair could just make believe I’m Council Member Wong for a second is that - is that I - for the first ten years, I was a tax auditor and they found boxes and boxes of cases in the basement that had to be addressed. It is impossible for you to fix a problem that has accumulated over so much time. So, that’s why I’m volunteering to come back. You need a swat team.
Okay.
I’m just suggesting.
For now I have my Chief Legal Counsel, she’s not a swat team but she’s close.

Yes, oh yeah, well, Council Member, thank you so much for giving us the opportunity to address this. We’ve got a swat team and that swat team is acting pursuant to the court order issued by Judge Loretta Preska in the LV case and we have transformed this work. I would love to share updated data with you. I think your data is out of date.

Uhm, because we are down to record turnaround time for issuing payments. Now, some providers do experience delays and most of where we see those delays happening is when they’re unable to provide us with required documentation such as a confirmation from a parent that the services have been provided. So, I’m aware that some providers are having that experience but in terms of when we get the paperwork that parties, that families are required to submit to us, we’re getting payment turned around in a matter of weeks.
I want to thank you for inviting me to come see you. It’s the first time in history that that has happened.
My goodness.
I’m very excited by the way, even if I don’t show up, even the fact that you invited me.
I’ll be there. I’ll be there.
No, I’m going to take you up on the offer.
Great, we’d love to show you our dashboards.
I want to. Thank you.
Good, thank you.
Thank you. Thank you Council Member. Council Member Epstein.

Thank you and I know you’ve been here a long time. So, I want to talk about uhm, so in my district, we see a lot of trouble early on in learning and we use a program called Literacy Academy that really helps kids get up to speed and we see that really transforming people's lives. I’m wondering where you are on expanding, ensuring that you know earlier on in their careers, we’re getting kids to learn to read earlier enough in their career Chancellor.

Alright, I’m sorry, look I think Literacy Academy is a strong forum. We at uhm, at our - at DOE, we’re really thinking about and have been over the last number of years, especially with uhm, New York City Reads in terms of early screening. Uhm, you know really thinking at making sure that our - we’re responding to our uhm -

Chancellor, can we expand things because I worry about Summer Rising. I worry that, that we’re not educating kids during Summer Rising and Literacy Academy is really a place

where we can do that and replaces programs like that. I’m wondering if we can be expanding that. We’re struggling to get enough resources where I live in District 1 and across my District.

Yeah, we can look into that. I do think last year in particular for the first time, we did incorporate uh literacy interventionists into Summer Rising program because we see that need there as well. And so, we can - we can talk more offline about Literacy Academy but I do recognize like you said, the need to think about early literacy and to make sure that we’re addressing needs earlier.
